The House of Windsor. The British royal family has ruled the United Kingdom and the Commonwealth since 1917, when they renamed themselves from the House of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha to distance themselves from Germany during World War I. Modern and adaptable, the Windsors have navigated the decline of empire, social upheaval, and constitutional monarchy while preserving their institution and cultural prestige into the twenty-first century.

King George V reigned from 1910 to 1935 and established a more restrained, conscientious style of monarchy after the flamboyance of his predecessor. Edward VIII reigned for only a few months in 1936 before abdicating in a constitutional crisis over his intention to marry Wallis Simpson, an American divorcée deemed unsuitable. His brother George VI reigned from 1936 to 1952. He restored dignity to the monarchy through World War II leadership and helped transition the British Empire to a Commonwealth. Elizabeth II reigned from 1952 to 2022 as the longest-reigning British monarch. She presided over decolonization, social change, and the modernization of the monarchy while maintaining its ceremonial role.

The Windsors adapted to democratic expectations and media scrutiny in ways earlier monarchies could not. The family became more visible and approachable. The Windsor dynasty reigns over the Commonwealth of Nations, with the sovereign as head of state in numerous countries beyond the United Kingdom as of the twenty-first century.
